newsitem.title: RUSSIA: India minister repeats objections to test ban pact.
newsitem.headline: India minister repeats objections to test ban pact.

text.p: Indian Foreign Minister I.K. Gujral on Monday reiterated his country's opposition to an international pact aimed at banning nuclear tests, Interfax news agency said.

"India cannot sign this document in its present form neither today nor later," it quoted Gujral as saying in reference to the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), which has already been signed by almost 140 countries.

"India favours any step aimed at destroying nuclear weapons," he added. "But we consider that the treaty in its current form is not comprehensive and bans only certain types of tests. That is why we oppose it."

Gujral arrived in Moscow on Sunday to take part in a two-day session of the Indo-Russian inter-governmental commission on trade, economic, scientific and cultural cooperation. He is due to leave Russia on Wednesday.
Russia, a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council and one the world's five recognized nuclear powers, strongly backs the CTBT pact.
But Moscow, keen to preserve traditionally close ties with India, has stopped short of openly criticising New Delhi for its controversial stance.

Political analysts in Moscow say Russia, which is strongly pressed by the United States to scrap its planned sale to India of two light-water reactors, is especially sensitive about issues of nuclear disarmament and control.
Indian PTI news agency quoted Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin as saying Moscow was planning to go ahead with the proposed $2.6 billion reactor sale.

PTI quoted Ilyushin, who on Monday addressed the opening of a two-day meeting of the inter-government commission, as saying a quick decision should be taken on the power station where the reactors would be installed.

The United States has objected to the reactor deal signed by India and the Soviet Union in 1988, saying it violated an agreement reached in 1992 by suppliers of nuclear technology, including Russia, not to sell to non-nuclear states.
Russian officials insist that the 1992 agreement should not be applied to the deal with India.

Earlier on Monday Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who met Gujral, said Moscow viewed his visit as important to preparations for a meeting between President Boris Yeltsin and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Gowda was due to visit Moscow in February but the visit was postponed after Yeltsin developed pneumonia last month. A new date for the visit has not yet been announced.
Yeltsin is now recovering from pneumonia at a residence outside Moscow.
